findings.title: Removing the multiple-provider error lets equal-order providers be picked silently (FIPS vs non-FIPS)
findings.body:
Before this change, `detectProvider` threw when more than one CryptoProvider was found. Now it sorts by `order()` and takes the first. `DefaultCryptoProvider`, `WildFlyElytronProvider` and `FIPS1402Provider` all return 200.

If two of them end up on the classpath (for example a misconfigured FIPS distribution that also ships the default crypto jar), the stable sort falls back to ServiceLoader/classpath order. One provider is chosen arbitrarily, and the conflict is reported only at debug level. A FIPS deployment could silently run with the non-FIPS BouncyCastle provider.

Suggested fix: keep failing (or at least warn loudly) when the top two providers share the same order. Only the lower-priority fallback (the authz-client provider at 100) should be ignored silently.

findings.title: New abstract interface method breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations
findings.body:
`int order()` is added as an abstract method on the public `CryptoProvider` SPI. Any external or custom implementation (custom crypto providers, the separate keycloak-client repository) will no longer compile. Already-compiled ones will throw `AbstractMethodError` when `CryptoIntegration.detectProvider` calls `order()` during sorting.

Suggested fix: declare it as a `default` method returning a neutral value (e.g. 0 or 200) to keep the SPI backward compatible.

findings.title: getBouncyCastleProvider returns the default KeyStore provider and builds a KeyStore on every call
findings.body:
`getBouncyCastleProvider()` returns `KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider()`, typically `SUN`. This is not a BouncyCastle provider.

Code that relies on `BouncyIntegration.PROVIDER` (derived from this method) will request algorithms from that provider by name. For example `KeyFactory.getInstance(alg, "SUN")` will fail with NoSuchAlgorithmException for most algorithms.

It also instantiates a new KeyStore on every call. Return a cached provider, and document clearly that this is not BC.

findings.title: Dead code: encoders created and discarded
findings.body: Lines 114-115 call `ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger)` and `ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger)` and throw away the results. The same encoders are built again inside `writeDerSeq` just below. This is leftover code that should be removed.

findings.title: Test uses a single default-size EC key for ES384/ES512, so P-384/P-521 paths are never exercised
findings.body:
The key pair is generated with `KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC")` using the default curve, typically P-256. That same key is used for ES256, ES384 and ES512, so r and s are always about 32 bytes.

Untested paths:
- 48- and 66-byte integers.
- The ES512 case, where the DER sequence exceeds 127 bytes and the long-form length code in `ASN1Encoder.writeLength` and `ASN1Decoder.readLength` is needed.

The test also only round-trips through the custom code. It never checks the DER output with `Signature.verify` or against the BC implementation, so a symmetric bug would pass.

Suggested fix: initialize the generator with the matching curve for each algorithm (secp256r1, secp384r1, secp521r1) and verify the re-encoded DER signature with the JDK.

findings.title: Indefinite-length (-1) handling yields incorrect reads
findings.body:
`readLength` returns -1 for indefinite-length encoding, and callers do not handle it.
- In `readSequence`, the loop exits immediately.
- In `readNext`, `length += reset()` produces a wrong small length, so `read(length)` returns a truncated element.
- In `readInteger`, `new byte[-1]` throws `NegativeArraySizeException`, an unchecked exception instead of `IOException`.

DER never allows indefinite length, so reject it explicitly with an `IOException`.
